title: Basis
body:
A **basis** for a [[Vector Space]] $V$ is a set of vectors that is both

1. **[[Linear Dependence|linearly independent]]** (no redundancy), and
2. **spanning** (reaches everything in $V$).

Those two conditions pull in opposite directions: spanning wants more vectors, independence
wants fewer. A basis is the exact point where they meet, which is why it is the central
definition of the chapter. **Not too few to reach everything, not so many that one is
redundant.**

## Why it is the right idea

If $\{\mathbf{b}_1, \dots, \mathbf{b}_n\}$ is a basis for $V$, then every $\mathbf{v} \in V$ can
be written as

$$
\mathbf{v} = c_1\mathbf{b}_1 + c_2\mathbf{b}_2 + \cdots + c_n\mathbf{b}_n
$$

in **exactly one way**. Spanning gives existence, independence gives uniqueness (two different
representations subtract to a non-trivial combination equal to $\mathbf{0}$, which independence
forbids). Those $c_i$ are the **coordinates** of $\mathbf{v}$ with respect to that basis.

So a basis is a coordinate system, and picking one turns abstract vectors into columns of
numbers you can compute with. **Coordinates depend on the basis, the vector does not.** The
arrow on the page is what it is; the numbers describing it change when you change the ruler.

## Standard basis

$\mathbb{R}^n$ has the obvious choice: $\mathbf{e}_1 = (1,0,\dots,0)$, up to
$\mathbf{e}_n = (0,\dots,0,1)$. Under it, a vector's coordinates are just its entries, which is
so convenient it disguises the fact that a choice was made.

Other spaces have standard bases too: $\{1, x, x^2\}$ for polynomials of degree $\leq 2$, and
the matrices with a single $1$ for $2\times 2$ matrices. Both are cases where the "vectors" look
nothing like arrows and the machinery works anyway.

## Dimension

**Every basis of $V$ has the same number of vectors**, and that number is $\dim V$. This is a
theorem, not a definition, and it is what makes dimension meaningful: it comes from the counting
fact in [[Linear Dependence]] that you cannot have more than $n$ independent vectors in an
$n$-dimensional space.

$$
\dim \mathbb{R}^n = n, \qquad \dim P_n = n+1, \qquad \dim M_{2\times 2} = 4
$$

The $P_n$ one catches people: degree $\leq 2$ needs $\{1, x, x^2\}$, which is three vectors.

Once you know $\dim V = n$, checking a basis gets cheaper. **For a set of exactly $n$ vectors in
an $n$-dimensional space, independent and spanning are equivalent**, so you only check one.
Usually independence, via [[Gaussian Elimination]] or a [[Determinant]].

## Finding one

- **From a spanning set that is too big**: row reduce, keep the vectors in the pivot columns,
  discard the rest.
- **For the [[Kernel and Range|kernel]] of $A$**: solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ and read off
  one basis vector per free variable.
- **For the column space of $A$**: reduce $A$ and take the **original** columns that ended up
  with pivots. Take the original ones, not the reduced ones; row operations preserve which
  columns are independent but not what they are.

## Orthonormal bases

A basis is **orthonormal** when every vector is a unit vector and every pair is orthogonal
([[Dot Product]] zero). These are the good ones, because finding coordinates stops being a
system to solve and becomes a projection:

$$
\mathbf{v} = (\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{b}_1)\mathbf{b}_1 + \cdots + (\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{b}_n)\mathbf{b}_n
$$

One dot product per coordinate instead of an $O(n^3)$ elimination. **This formula is the reason
[[Fourier Series]] works.** The sines and cosines are an orthonormal basis for a space of
functions, and a [[Fourier Coefficients|Fourier coefficient]] is exactly one of those dot
products, with the sum replaced by an integral. See [[Orthogonal Functions]].

[[Gram-Schmidt]] is the procedure that turns any basis into an orthonormal one by repeatedly
subtracting off projections; [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE|MATH 2303]] uses it for the QR
decomposition, and takes the truncation property above into [[Low-Rank Approximation]]. See
[[Orthonormal Basis]].

## Change of basis

Coordinates in one basis convert to another by multiplying by a change-of-basis matrix, whose
columns are the old basis vectors written in the new one. This is the machinery
[[Diagonalization]] runs on: $A = PDP^{-1}$ says "change into the eigenvector basis, where the
transformation is a simple scaling, do it, and change back". **Choosing the right basis is how
you make a hard problem easy**, and it is the most transferable idea in the course.

## Related

- [[Vector Space]], [[Linear Dependence]], [[Dot Product]]
- [[Kernel and Range]] and rank-nullity, which is a statement about dimensions
- [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]]: the eigenvectors, when there are enough of them, form the
  most useful basis a matrix has
